name: Clownfish
habitat: Sheltered reef flats and lagoons, living inside host anemones
description: Bright orange with white bands, clownfish live their whole lives partnered with a single sea anemone. A special mucus coating protects them from the anemone's stinging cells. They are territorial and will boldly inspect snorkellers passing near their home.
funFact: All clownfish are born male — the dominant fish in a group can change sex to become female.

name: Blue Tang
diet: Algae it grazes off coral and rocks
habitat: Coral reefs, often in loose schools
description: Juveniles are vivid yellow; adults shift to royal blue with a yellow tail spine. Blue tangs graze algae that would otherwise smother coral, making them vital reef gardeners.
funFact: The 'surgeonfish' name comes from a scalpel-sharp spine at the base of the tail — handle a tangled one with care.

name: Queen Angelfish
habitat: Deep reef slopes and ledges, often in pairs
description: One of the Caribbean's most striking fish: electric blue and yellow with a dark crown-like spot. Usually seen in pairs patrolling the reef, they are curious and will approach snorkellers slowly.
funFact: They are known to hybridise with the closely related blue angelfish.

name: Stoplight Parrotfish
habitat: Coral reefs from shallow flats to fore-reefs
description: Parrotfish crunch coral with beak-like teeth to reach algae, then excrete the grit as sand. Males shimmer turquoise and pink; females and juveniles are mottled red-brown.
funFact: A single large parrotfish can produce hundreds of kilograms of beach sand each year.

name: Sergeant Major
habitat: Shallow reefs, jetties and rocky areas in huge schools
description: Named for its five black stripes, this hardy damselfish forms pulsing schools over shallow reefs. During breeding, males turn bluish and fiercely guard egg patches on rock faces.
funFact: The males guard their purple egg patches so diligently they will even chase much larger fish away.

name: Great Barracuda
habitat: Reefs, seagrass beds and open water near shore
description: A sleek, silver torpedo with an underslung jaw of jagged teeth. Barracuda are curious and may shadow snorkellers, but attacks on people are extremely rare. Avoid wearing flashy jewellery that can look like prey.
funFact: Barracuda have no swim bladder, so they must keep swimming — you'll rarely see one hover.

name: Nassau Grouper
habitat: Coral reefs and rocky ledges
description: A thick-bodied, curious reef predator with distinctive 'tattoo' bars across its head. Nassau groupers famously approach divers and can change colour to communicate mood.
funFact: Once a year, thousands gather at the same spawning sites on the full moon — sadly, this predictability has made them easy to overfish.

name: Moorish Idol
habitat: Clear reef flats and slopes
description: Elegant black, white and yellow bands with a long dorsal filament. They drift in pairs or small groups along the reef crest, picking at sponges in crevices.
funFact: Despite the name, they are unrelated to the 'Gill' character fish they inspired in Finding Nemo.

name: Blue Regal Tang
habitat: Outer reef slopes, schooling above coral heads
description: The vivid cobalt-blue surgeonfish with a black palette marking and yellow tail. They form loose feeding schools that hover above the reef, drifting with the current.
funFact: Juveniles are bright yellow with blue fins before growing into adult colours.

name: Titan Triggerfish
habitat: Sandy reef flats and coral gardens
description: Large, leathery and territorial. When guarding their nest chamber, titan triggerfish will aggressively charge intruders — including snorkellers — and can deliver a serious bite.
funFact: Nesting females bite and ram anything above the nest, so swim backwards and away along the seabed — the territory is an upward cone.
imageCredit: (c) Jan Ebr & Ivana Ebrová, some rights reserved (CC BY)

name: Blacktip Reef Shark
habitat: Shallow lagoons and reef flats
description: A slender, shy shark with unmistakable black fin tips, commonly seen patrolling shallow lagoons in small groups. They avoid people and are easily startled by splashing.
funFact: Some can speed-burst at nearly 20 km/h when chasing prey over the reef flat.

name: Whitetip Reef Shark
habitat: Caves and overhangs, resting by day
description: Recognisable by white-tipped dorsal and tail fins, these sharks rest in caves during the day and hunt alone at night. Snorkellers often see them lying quietly under ledges.
funFact: They can pump water over their gills, letting them rest motionless on the seabed — most sharks must swim to breathe.

name: Reef Manta Ray
habitat: Cleaning stations and plankton-rich coastal waters
description: Graceful giants that glide on 5 m wings, barrel-rolling to feed on plankton. Each manta's belly spots are unique, like a fingerprint. Completely safe to swim alongside.
funFact: Mantas have the largest brain-to-body ratio of any fish and appear to recognise individual divers.

name: Green Sea Turtle
habitat: Seagrass meadows, lagoons and reef flats
description: The classic reef turtle: paddling serenely over seagrass beds or resting under coral ledges. Keep distance, never touch or chase, and give them room to surface and breathe.
funFact: Green turtles can hold their breath for hours while resting — but a startled swimmer can stress them into fleeing.

name: Hawksbill Turtle
habitat: Coral reefs, especially crevices and drop-offs
description: Smaller than the green turtle with a hawk-like beak and amber shell plates. Hawksbills are the reef's sponge-eaters, keeping fast-growing sponges from overgrowing coral.
funFact: Their beautiful 'tortoiseshell' pattern made them a target for the souvenir trade, which devastated populations.

name: Bottlenose Dolphin
habitat: Coastal bays, estuaries and open water
description: Playful, social and intelligent, bottlenose dolphins sometimes approach swimmers and surfers to surf bow waves. Enjoy from a distance — they are wild animals with their own schedules.
funFact: Dolphins sleep with half their brain at a time, keeping one eye open.

name: Lionfish
habitat: Reef crevices, overhangs and wrecks
description: Striped red-and-white lionfish with feather-like pectoral fins and venomous dorsal spines. In the Caribbean and Atlantic they are an invasive plague that devours young reef fish.
funFact: A sting is extremely painful but rarely deadly — heat (45°C water) on the wound breaks down the venom.
imageCredit: Photo by Jens Petersen, Edited by User:Olegiwit (cloned in part of fins) and Fir0002 (removed spots and noise)

name: Reef Stonefish
habitat: Coral rubble, sandy flats and weedy areas
description: The most venomous fish known: a lumpy, camouflaged ambush predator that looks exactly like a rock. Dorsal spines inject a severe venom — shuffle your feet and never grab 'rocks'.
funFact: Stonefish can survive 24 hours out of water — a stranded one is still dangerous.

name: Giant Moray Eel
habitat: Caves and holes in the reef
description: A thick green eel with a menacing mouth permanently agape — it's just breathing. Morays are shy and retreat into holes, but feeding or provoking them can cause serious bites.
funFact: Morays have a second set of jaws in their throat that lunges forward to drag prey in.

name: Common Octopus
habitat: Rocky reefs, lairs marked by shell middens
description: A master of camouflage that shifts colour and skin texture in a heartbeat. Octopuses are curious and intelligent; if one studies you from its den, hold still and let it look.
funFact: An octopus has three hearts and blue, copper-based blood.

name: Broadclub Cuttlefish
habitat: Coral reefs and sandy slopes
description: The chameleon of the sea: cuttlefish ripple waves of colour across their skin to hypnotise prey and talk to each other. They hover like small hovercraft, steering with skirt-like fins.
funFact: Cuttlefish are colourblind — yet they match background colours perfectly using polarised light cues.

name: Box Jellyfish
size: Bell to 30 cm, tentacles to 3 m
habitat: Warm coastal waters, especially after rain and on calm evenings
description: Transparent and nearly invisible in the water, box jellyfish are among the most venomous animals in the sea. In northern Australia stinger season runs roughly October to May — swim inside stinger nets or wear a full stinger suit.
funFact: Unlike most jellyfish, box jellyfish have eyes — 24 of them, some with lenses and retinas.
imageCredit:
Avispa marina.jpg: Guido Gautsch, Toyota, Japan
derivative work: Mithril (talk)

name: Moon Jellyfish
habitat: Calm coastal waters, drifting in groups
description: A translucent saucer with four horseshoe gonads visible on top. Its sting is mild for most people — a slight tingle on sensitive skin. Swarms can fill quiet bays after onshore winds.
funFact: Moon jellies have been studied by NASA — thousands flew aboard space shuttle Columbia in 1991.

name: Starry Pufferfish
habitat: Reef slopes and lagoons
description: A slow, charming reef resident that inflates into a spiky balloon when threatened. Their flesh and organs contain tetrodotoxin, a deadly poison — never touch or eat them.
funFact: Tetrodotoxin is up to 1,000 times more toxic than cyanide, with no known antidote.

name: Raccoon Butterflyfish
habitat: Reef slopes and lagoons, often in pairs
description: Butterflyfish are the reef's ballet dancers — flat, vividly patterned fish that flit between coral branches in pairs. Their 'eyeband' patterns confuse predators about which end is the head.
funFact: Butterflyfish are so faithful to their partners that marine biologists use them as a gauge of reef health.

name: Bluestreak Cleaner Wrasse
diet: Parasites and dead skin picked off clients
habitat: Fixed 'cleaning stations' on the reef
description: These tiny wrasse set up service points where big fish — even sharks — queue up to have parasites nibbled off. They perform a hypnotic zigzag dance to advertise.
funFact: Some sneaky blenny fish mimic cleaners, then take a bite of fin instead — the reef's own con artists.

name: Humphead Wrasse
diet: Molluscs, fish, starfish and even toxic crown-of-thorns
habitat: Steep outer reef slopes
description: The giant of the wrasse family, with a distinct hump above the eyes and pouty lips. These gentle, inquisitive giants may follow snorkellers around the reef like oversized puppies.
funFact: They are one of the few predators that eat crown-of-thorns starfish, protecting corals from outbreaks.

name: Garibaldi
habitat: Kelp forests and rocky reefs
description: California's state marine fish: a blazing orange damselfish that darts through kelp gardens. Males cultivate neat red-algae lawns to impress females and guard the nest fiercely.
funFact: The male chirps at intruders by grinding throat teeth together — a sound divers can hear underwater.

name: Leafy Sea Dragon
habitat: Kelp and seagrass in southern Australia
description: A seahorse relative draped in leaf-like appendages that sway with the kelp, making it nearly invisible. Look closely — spotting one is a badge of honour for snorkellers.
funFact: The male carries the bright pink eggs on a brood patch under his tail until they hatch.

name: Blue Groper
habitat: Rocky reefs and kelp beds
description: Big, friendly and famously inquisitive — blue gropers follow snorkellers around New South Wales reefs like tour guides. Despite the name, females are brownish and juveniles green.
funFact: They crunch sea urchins with plate-like teeth, keeping kelp forests grazed clean.
imageCredit: (c) Andrew Harvey, some rights reserved (CC BY)

name: Dusky Grouper
habitat: Rocky reefs and wrecks
description: The Mediterranean's gentle giant, often found resting beside boulders and approaching divers with calm curiosity. Long-lived and slow to reproduce, it has declined from overfishing.
funFact: Dusky groupers start life female and turn male as they grow — like many groupers.

name: Mediterranean Parrotfish
habitat: Rocky and Posidonia seabeds
description: Females are a rosy red-orange; males a slate blue-grey with a bright tail edge. Like their tropical cousins, they graze algae and help keep Mediterranean rocky reefs balanced.
funFact: Until genetics settled it, scientists argued for decades whether the colourful sexes were separate species.

name: Ballan Wrasse
habitat: Kelp and rocky reefs
description: A stocky, thick-lipped wrasse in mossy greens and blues that crushes shellfish with strong throat teeth. Often tame around snorkellers in the northeast Atlantic and Mediterranean.
funFact: Ballan wrasse change colour with age and sex — and can live more than 30 years.

name: Powder Blue Tang
diet: Algae grazed from rocks and dead coral
habitat: Clear reef flats and crests in strong light
description: A neon-blue surgeonfish with a jet-black face, white throat and bright yellow dorsal fin. Powder blue tangs patrol shallow reef crests in loose groups, grazing algae in the surge. The scalpel-like spine at the tail base is strictly for defence.
funFact: They often team up with other surgeonfish species, forming mixed grazing herds that overwhelm the defences of territorial damselfish.

name: Yellow Tang
habitat: Coral reefs and rocky areas of the central Pacific
description: The brilliant lemon-yellow fish that lights up Hawaiian reefs. Yellow tangs browse algae in busy schools and use the sharp white spine at the base of the tail to settle disputes. They are a favourite of snorkellers for their colour and curiosity.
funFact: At night their yellow fades to a dull, ghostly grey with a white stripe — camouflage for sleeping in the reef.

name: Emperor Angelfish
habitat: Rich coral reefs, often beneath ledges and in caves
description: Adults are a royal blue-and-yellow striped maze with a dark mask and electric-blue rim; juveniles are deep blue with concentric white rings. Emperor angelfish are shy but curious, usually seen in pairs near shelter.
funFact: The juvenile's swirling white rings are thought to mimic a large eye, confusing predators about which end is the head.

name: Clown Triggerfish
habitat: Clear lagoons and outer reef slopes
description: A bold, pattern-heavy triggerfish: black body, white-spotted belly, yellow reticulated back and a pale band across the snout. It blows jets of water to flip urchins and crabs over, then crushes them with strong jaws. Nesting fish can be defensive.
funFact: The triggerfish's name comes from a locking dorsal spine it can erect to wedge itself into a crevice — predators cannot pull it out.

name: Picasso Triggerfish
diet: Algae, crustaceans, worms and sea urchins
habitat: Sandy reef flats, rubble and seagrass edges
description: Painted in bold blocks of cream, black, blue and yellow, this triggerfish looks like modern art. It grubs through sand and rubble for invertebrates and guards its nesting patch with surprising aggression, sometimes nipping at fins or cameras.
funFact: Picasso triggerfish build and tend nests in sand, and both parents may defend the eggs until they hatch.

name: Blue-green Chromis
habitat: Branching coral thickets on sheltered reefs
description: Small, shimmering damselfish that gather in glittering clouds above staghorn and cauliflower coral. When a predator approaches, the whole school folds back into the branches in a heartbeat. They are a reassuring sight on a healthy shallow reef.
funFact: Males turn a darker blue and clean a patch of coral to court females, then guard the eggs until they hatch.
imageCredit: (c) Debra Baker, some rights reserved (CC BY)

name: Bumphead Parrotfish
diet: Algae scraped from coral and rock
habitat: Outer reef slopes, lagoons and passes
description: The largest parrotfish, with a steep forehead and a beak powerful enough to bite coral. Schools crunch across the reef in a visible cloud of limestone dust. They are slow-growing and sleep in caves in groups, which makes them vulnerable to fishing.
funFact: A single bumphead parrotfish can produce more than a tonne of coral sand a year — much of the beach you lie on may have passed through one.

name: Spotted Eagle Ray
habitat: Reef flats, lagoons and sandy channels
description: A soaring ray with white spots on a dark back, a long snout and a whip-like tail. Eagle rays glide in formation over sandy flats, using their snout to root out shellfish. Their tail carries venomous spines — never swim over or corner one.
funFact: Like a fingerprint, the spot pattern on an eagle ray's back is unique to each individual.
imageCredit: the manta ray had a family

name: Nurse Shark
habitat: Sandy flats, seagrass beds and reef caves
description: A slow, bottom-dwelling shark with rounded fins and barbels under its snout. Nurse sharks rest in piles under ledges by day and hunt by suction at night. They are docile but should never be grabbed or fed — even a sleepy shark can bite in self-defence.
funFact: They can pump water over their gills while lying still, so unlike many sharks they do not need to keep swimming to breathe.

name: Mandarinfish
habitat: Rubble and coral heads in sheltered lagoons
description: One of the most colourful animals on the reef: a tiny dragonet painted in psychedelic swirls of blue, orange and green. Mandarinfish creep over rubble, hunting microscopic prey. They are easiest to spot at dusk, when pairs rise together to spawn.
funFact: Their colour comes from pigment cells in the skin rather than reflective crystals, making them one of the few truly blue animals.

name: Red Sea Bannerfish
habitat: Reef slopes, lagoons and coral gardens
description: A white, black-banded butterflyfish with a long, trailing dorsal filament that looks like a banner. Red Sea bannerfish often hover in pairs or small groups, picking plankton from the current. Their false 'eye' near the tail confuses predators.
funFact: The long dorsal filament is not just decoration — a predator that strikes at it is left with a mouthful of fin while the fish escapes.

name: Yellow Boxfish
habitat: Reef flats, lagoons and sandy slopes
description: A living cube: bright yellow with black spots, encased in a rigid bony box. Juveniles are tiny, rounded and impossibly cute; adults become longer and duller. When stressed, boxfish release ostracitoxin, a poison that can kill nearby fish in a confined space.
funFact: Their boxy body is surprisingly hydrodynamic — engineers have studied boxfish shapes to design more efficient cars.

name: Banggai Cardinalfish
habitat: Shallow seagrass and coral around the Banggai Islands
description: A silver fish with bold black stripes and glittering white spots, found only around a handful of Indonesian islands. It shelters among the spines of sea urchins and long-tentacled anemones. Its tiny range and popularity in the aquarium trade make it a conservation concern.
funFact: The male broods the eggs in his mouth for nearly a month — and the young stay close to their father long after hatching.

name: French Angelfish
diet: Sponges, tunicates, algae and small invertebrates
habitat: Coral reefs, sea-fan gardens and rocky ledges
description: A bold black fish with yellow-rimmed scales and a bright yellow face. French angelfish usually swim in pairs and patrol a home territory, picking sponges and algae from the reef. Juveniles look completely different, with dark bodies and yellow bars.
funFact: Young French angelfish act as cleaners, picking parasites and loose skin from larger fish.

name: Foureye Butterflyfish
diet: Coral polyps, worms and small crustaceans
habitat: Shallow reefs, patch reefs and seagrass edges
description: White with fine diagonal lines and a large dark spot near the tail, this small butterflyfish often moves in pairs. It picks at coral polyps and small invertebrates and will shelter among branching corals when approached.
funFact: The dark spot on the tail is a false eye, meant to make a predator unsure which end is the head.

name: Yellowtail Snapper
diet: Zooplankton, small fish, shrimp and crabs
habitat: Reef slopes, seagrass beds and sandy channels
description: A slender silver snapper with a yellow stripe along its side and a vivid yellow tail. Yellowtail snapper often hover in loose schools above the reef, darting after plankton and small prey.
funFact: The bright tail may help school members keep formation in dim light or turbid water.

name: Hogfish
diet: Molluscs, crabs, sea urchins and worms
habitat: Reefs, rubble and seagrass beds
description: A large wrasse with a long snout and fleshy lips, built for rooting prey out of sand and rubble. Its colour ranges from pale grey to mottled red, and it can be surprisingly curious around snorkellers.
funFact: All hogfish start life female; the largest individuals change into males.

name: Queen Triggerfish
diet: Sea urchins, crabs, molluscs and tunicates
habitat: Reefs, seagrass beds and sandy patches
description: One of the most striking Caribbean triggerfish, with blue lines, yellow edges and a deeply forked tail. It uses powerful jaws and a knack for flipping urchins to get at the softer underside.
funFact: It can lock its first dorsal spine upright as a defence and move each eye independently.

name: Balloonfish
diet: Crabs, snails, sea urchins and hermit crabs
habitat: Reef flats, seagrass beds and mangrove edges
description: A mottled brown porcupinefish covered in short spines. When threatened it gulps water, balloons up and points the spines outward. Its skin and organs contain tetrodotoxin, so it should never be handled or eaten.
funFact: Its beak-like teeth can crush snail shells and sea-urchin tests with ease.

name: Spotted Garden Eel
habitat: Sandy burrows in reef flats and seagrass patches
description: Slender white eels with black spots rise from sandy burrows in swaying colonies, snatching plankton from the current. They are shy and disappear into the sand in a blink when a diver comes too close.
funFact: Garden eels rarely leave their burrows and can reverse into them tail-first.

name: Harlequin Tuskfish
diet: Molluscs, crabs, worms and sea urchins
habitat: Coral reefs, rubble and sandy patches
description: A reef wrasse with vivid orange and white bands, blue lines and protruding tusk-like teeth. It patrols rubble and sand, turning over rocks and shells to find hard-shelled prey.
funFact: Its blue-tipped tusks are used to flip rocks and crack open shells.

name: Bluespotted Ribbontail Ray
diet: Worms, crabs, shrimp and small fish
habitat: Sandy and rubbly reef flats
description: A small round ray covered in electric-blue spots, with a folded ribbon-like tail. It rests under ledges or half-buried in sand and is best admired from a distance: the tail carries a venomous spine.
funFact: The blue spots are not decoration; they signal that the tail barb is highly venomous.

name: Warty Frogfish
habitat: Reef walls, sponges and rubble
description: A lumpy, warty ambush predator that looks more like an encrusted sponge than a fish. It waits motionless with a fishing-rod lure over its mouth, then strikes with a sudden gulp.
funFact: Its mouth can open so wide that it swallows prey almost as large as itself.

name: Giant Trevally
habitat: Reef passes, drop-offs and lagoons
description: A powerful silver predator with a steep forehead and a deeply forked tail. Giant trevally hunt along reef edges and in passes, sometimes in loose groups, and can move with startling speed.
funFact: Large individuals can darken to almost black, especially when excited or hunting.

name: Banded Sea Krait
habitat: Coral reefs, rocky shores and sea caves
description: A black-and-white banded sea snake with a flattened paddle-like tail. It breathes air but hunts underwater, and returns to land to rest, digest and lay eggs. It is highly venomous but usually shy.
funFact: Sea kraits can spend long periods at sea but must come ashore to lay their eggs.

name: Red Sea Clownfish
habitat: Coral reefs with host anemones
description: An orange-brown clownfish with two white bands, living in a partnership with a host anemone. It rarely strays far from the tentacles that protect it from predators.
funFact: It is the only clownfish native to the Red Sea and the Gulf of Aden.

name: Arabian Angelfish
habitat: Coral reefs, lagoons and rocky ledges
description: A dark blue-purple angelfish with a bold yellow tail and a yellow crescent across its side. It grazes on sponges and algae and often patrols a regular route along the reef.
funFact: Juveniles are so differently patterned that they were once described as a separate species.

name: Sohal Surgeonfish
habitat: Shallow reef flats and surge zones
description: A striped surgeonfish with a bright orange tail and a scalpel-like spine at the base of the tail. It grazes algae in shallow, wave-washed areas and is famously territorial.
funFact: It can slash with the folded spine on its tail when defending an algae patch.

name: Mediterranean Damselfish
habitat: Rocky reefs, seagrass beds and wrecks
description: A small dark damselfish that gathers in clouds above Mediterranean reefs. Males guard nests during the breeding season, and the whole group can vanish into crevices at the first sign of danger.
funFact: Nesting males turn almost black and fiercely chase away intruders.
imageCredit: (c) Julien Renoult, some rights reserved (CC BY)

name: Ornate Wrasse
habitat: Rocky reefs and seagrass meadows
description: A restless wrasse patterned in green, blue and orange. It weaves through rocky reefs and seagrass, inspecting crevices for small invertebrates and occasionally picking parasites from other fish.
funFact: Like many wrasses, females can transform into brightly coloured males as they grow.

name: Salema Porgy
habitat: Seagrass meadows, rocky reefs and sandy shores
description: A silver porgy with golden horizontal stripes, usually seen in schools grazing over seagrass and algae. It is one of the few fish that regularly eats seagrass leaves.
funFact: Its gut hosts microbes that help break down tough seagrass, a rare talent among fish.

name: Mediterranean Moray
habitat: Rocky crevices and wrecks
description: A mottled brown moray with pale yellow eyes, usually seen with just its head showing from a rocky hole. It opens and closes its mouth to breathe, which can look threatening, but it prefers to retreat.
funFact: A second set of jaws deep in its throat helps pull food down after the first bite.

name: King Angelfish
habitat: Rocky reefs and coral communities
description: A deep-bodied angelfish with a blue-brown body, a white vertical bar and a yellow tail. It is a common sight around rocky reefs in the tropical eastern Pacific and often swims in pairs.
funFact: Its species name, passer, refers to the sparrow-like markings near its eyes.

name: Cortez Rainbow Wrasse
habitat: Rocky and coral reefs
description: A small wrasse painted in pink, yellow, blue and green, constantly on the move over eastern Pacific reefs. It picks plankton and tiny animals from the water and from the reef surface.
funFact: Large males are far more colourful than females and guard spawning territories.
imageCredit: LASZLO ILYES from Cleveland, Ohio, USA

name: Yellowtail Surgeonfish
habitat: Rocky reefs and surge zones
description: A grey surgeonfish with a yellow tail and three bony plates along the side of its tail base. It grazes algae in shallow, wave-exposed areas and often gathers in groups.
funFact: Unlike most surgeonfish, which carry a single scalpel on each side, this species has three.

name: Mexican Hogfish
diet: Crabs, molluscs, sea urchins and worms
habitat: Rocky reefs and sand channels
description: A large eastern Pacific wrasse with a long snout and prominent canine teeth. Mature males are reddish with a dark head, while females and juveniles are yellow-pink with dark stripes.
funFact: Like many wrasses, it changes both sex and colour as it grows.

name: Panamic Green Moray
habitat: Rocky crevices and coral reefs
description: A greenish-brown moray with a blunt snout, commonly seen peering from holes in eastern Pacific reefs. It hunts at night and relies on smell to find fish and crustaceans.
funFact: Morays sometimes hunt alongside groupers, using head shakes to signal a hidden prey item.

name: California Sheephead
diet: Sea urchins, crabs, snails and barnacles
habitat: Kelp forests and rocky reefs
description: A kelp-forest wrasse with a black body, white chin and red head in mature males; females are pink-brown. Its strong jaws crush sea urchins, making it an important guardian of kelp beds.
funFact: By controlling urchin numbers, sheephead help keep kelp forests from being grazed bare.

name: Weedy Seadragon
habitat: Kelp beds, seagrass and rocky reefs
description: A reddish-brown seadragon with yellow leaf-like flaps that blur its outline among kelp. It drifts slowly and uses a long tubular snout to suck up small crustaceans.
funFact: Males carry the eggs on a brood patch beneath the tail, not in a pouch like seahorses.

name: Eastern Blue Devil
habitat: Rocky reefs, caves and ledges
description: A striking blue fish with yellow fins and a pale stripe along its side, usually found lurking in caves and under ledges. It is shy and often seen only as a head peering from the dark.
funFact: It is a protected species in New South Wales waters.

name: Port Jackson Shark
diet: Sea urchins, crabs, molluscs and small fish
habitat: Rocky reefs, seagrass beds and sandy flats
description: A blunt-headed shark with a harness-like pattern of dark stripes across its back. It rests on the bottom during the day and is often encountered motionless under ledges or in seagrass.
funFact: Its flat, molar-like teeth are made for crushing urchins and shellfish.

name: Silver Drummer
habitat: Rocky reefs and kelp beds
description: A silver-grey schooling fish with a steep forehead and a small mouth. Silver drummer graze algae from rocky reefs and kelp beds, often in loose groups that move with the surge.
funFact: It can ferment algae in its gut, a rare way of extracting energy from tough plant material.

name: Cuckoo Wrasse
habitat: Rocky reefs, wrecks and maerl beds
description: A colourful north-east Atlantic wrasse. Females are orange with dark spots, while mature males are blue with bright orange markings. It picks small animals from rocky surfaces and retreats into crevices at night.
funFact: All cuckoo wrasses begin as females, and the largest change into males.

name: Tompot Blenny
habitat: Rocky crevices and under ledges
description: A mottled brown blenny with branched tentacles above its eyes, usually seen peering from a crevice. It rarely strays far from home and will retreat tail-first if approached too closely.
funFact: Its eyebrow-like tentacles help break up its outline against the rock.

name: European Conger
habitat: Rocky reefs, wrecks and burrows
description: A large grey eel-like fish that hides in holes and wrecks by day and hunts at night. It has a powerful bite and should never be fed or cornered by divers.
funFact: The largest conger eels can weigh more than 50 kg.

name: Atlantic Mackerel
habitat: Open water, often close to coast in summer
description: A streamlined blue-green fish with dark wavy stripes along its back, usually seen in fast-moving schools. It feeds on plankton and small fish and is a favourite prey for larger predators.
funFact: It has no swim bladder, so it must keep swimming to avoid sinking.
